claims.text: Applying a chromium-rich PVD coating to SS304 will improve its corrosion resistance in extreme environments.
The initial material is austenitic SS304 in the annealed condition.
The initial SS304 surface roughness is 0.1 μm.
The initial steel contains 18% Cr, 8% Ni, and balance Fe.
A 2 μm chromium-rich coating will be deposited by PVD at 500°C.
Corrosion performance will be evaluated in 3.5% NaCl at 80°C for 100 hours.
Exposure to 3.5% NaCl at 80°C for 100 hours simulates a marine environment.
The chromium-rich coating promotes formation of a chromium oxide layer.
The chromium oxide layer acts as a protective barrier.
The chromium oxide barrier reduces diffusion of corrosive species, including chloride ions, into the steel substrate.
Reduced diffusion of corrosive species decreases the corrosion rate.
The coating will reduce the corrosion rate by 30% relative to uncoated SS304.
The uncoated corrosion rate is 1.2 mm/year under the stated exposure conditions.
The coated corrosion rate will be 0.8 mm/year under the stated exposure conditions.
The coating thickness can be optimized within 1–5 μm to maximize corrosion resistance.
Alloy composition, surface preparation, and environmental conditions may affect the outcome.
Uncoated SS304 exposed under identical conditions will serve as the control.
The hypothesis is falsified unless the coated sample's corrosion rate is at least 0.5 mm/year lower than that of the uncoated sample after 100 hours.

contradictions.description: A decrease from 1.2 to 0.8 mm/year is 0.4 mm/year, or approximately 33.3%, rather than the stated 30%.

The predicted decrease is only 0.4 mm/year, while the falsification rule requires a decrease of at least 0.5 mm/year. Thus, the stated predicted outcome would falsify the hypothesis under its own rule.
